topic.title: Pancreas — chronic disease, cysts and tumors
topic.scopeIn: Chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic insufficiency, neoplastic cysts, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine tumors and pancreatic resection complications.
topic.scopeOut: Acute pancreatitis and inflammatory collections belong to pancreas-acute-pancreatitis. General endocrine syndromes belong to adrenal-men-endocrine.
topic.priorityReason: Cancer, cyst risk and chronic-disease operations need coverage beyond recognition and referral.
researchAgenda: Chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
topic.coverageReason: At most four distinct live clinical concept identities cover this scope. Variants repeat those identities.
topic.testingWeightBasis: Owner-directed editorial estimate of general-surgery testing relevance. No exam percentages or official blueprint weights are asserted.

release.catalogRegistryMeaning: 610 registered concept identities include 156 with no live node. Active coverage uses the 454 primaryConceptId identities actually scored in default-release nodes.

concepts.displayName: Recurrent postoperative pancreatic-fluid evaluation
concepts.learningObjective: Use recurrent enzyme-rich postoperative drainage and cross-sectional findings to select duct mapping before another drainage procedure.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Scored-objective override after reading the concept objective.

concepts.displayName: A pancreatic cyst that predates pancreatitis
concepts.learningObjective: Reassess the premise of inflammatory-collection drainage when prior imaging shows the pancreatic cyst existed before the pancreatitis episode.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: A drainage referral with two pancreatic lesions
concepts.learningObjective: Identify A as the lesion that predates pancreatitis and separate it from B's later post-necrotizing collection. Redirect the referral to characterization before planning entry into A.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: MCN-compatible pancreatic-cyst pattern recognition
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize a body or tail cyst without main-duct communication as MCN-compatible without claiming definitive histology or automatic resection.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: MRCP duct assessment for an indeterminate pancreatic cyst
concepts.learningObjective: Use MRI/MRCP to assess communication between an indeterminate pancreatic cyst and the main duct.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy for resectable tail adenocarcinoma
concepts.learningObjective: Select oncologic distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy when a fit patient with pancreatic-tail adenocarcinoma has been judged resectable and is proceeding to surgery.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

question.patientPresentation: A fit patient with biopsy-confirmed, resectable pancreatic-tail adenocarcinoma and no distant metastases asks whether the planned distal resection ordinarily preserves the spleen.
question.stem: Which explanation should you give this patient?

answerChoices.label: The oncologic distal resection ordinarily includes splenectomy
Spleen preservation is standard for confirmed tail adenocarcinoma
answerChoices.distractorRationale: That generalization conflicts with the standard oncologic distal resection for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

answerChoices.label: A Whipple removes the pancreatic tail while preserving the spleen
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A Whipple is a pancreatic-head operation and does not describe resection of an isolated tail tumor.

answerChoices.label: Total pancreatectomy is required whenever the spleen is removed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Splenectomy with a distal pancreatic resection does not require removal of the entire pancreas.

question.explanation: For confirmed pancreatic-tail adenocarcinoma selected for resection, the standard oncologic distal operation ordinarily includes splenectomy. This does not generalize the same rule to benign distal lesions or other diagnoses.

question.patientPresentation: A hospital pancreatic-surgery conference reviews a medically fit patient with biopsy-confirmed, resectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma and no distant metastases. The operative team is matching tumor location to resection.
question.stem: Which location-operation pair is correct?

answerChoices.label: Pancreatic tail: distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy
Pancreatic tail: pancreaticoduodenectomy with splenic preservation
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Pancreaticoduodenectomy is not the anatomic resection for an isolated tail cancer.

answerChoices.label: Pancreatic head: distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Distal pancreatectomy does not remove the pancreatic head and uncinate process.

answerChoices.label: Pancreatic tail: total pancreatectomy based solely on location
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An isolated resectable tail location does not by itself justify total pancreatectomy.

question.explanation: A resectable pancreatic-tail adenocarcinoma is matched to oncologic distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy. Head or uncinate cancers use pancreaticoduodenectomy, and tail location alone is not an indication for total pancreatectomy.

decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should guide the next drainage plan in {patientName}'s hospital record?

answerChoices.label: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography test
answerChoices.rationale: The recurrent enzyme-rich cavity raises a continuing pancreatic source question; duct anatomy can change whether another drain is temporary or a duct-directed strategy is needed.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen
answerChoices.rationale: CT has already characterized the current cavity and viable gland. Repeating the same broad study is less useful for the remaining duct-planning question.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography test
answerChoices.rationale: An invasive duct procedure can have a therapeutic role, but choosing it before noninvasive mapping commits to an approach before the relevant anatomy is established.

decisionNodes.explanation: The CT has answered the broad collection question. Reaccumulation after drainage and enzyme-rich fluid make the persistent pancreatic source consequential. MRI/MRCP maps the duct before selecting the next drainage strategy. This does not establish disconnection from the CT or prescribe an endoscopic intervention before mapping.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old woman, has early satiety and a body-tail pancreatic cyst without demonstrated main-duct communication. A recent pancreatitis admission led to a proposed cyst-drainage referral. Her surgeon obtains an older scan showing the same cyst before she had ever developed pancreatitis; there is no documented diagnosis explaining its origin.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next plan fits {patientName}'s symptoms and the chronology of her pancreatic imaging?

answerChoices.label: Refer to the pancreatic cyst clinic
answerChoices.rationale: The pre-existing lesion cannot be assigned an inflammatory origin from the later pancreatitis event. Its cystic-neoplasm differential needs assessment before that drainage pathway.

answerChoices.label: Arrange pancreatic cyst drainage by endoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: This retains an unverified origin despite the older scan; symptoms do not resolve the classification question.

answerChoices.label: Arrange pancreatic cyst resection for cancer

decisionNodes.stem: Which next investigation should guide {patientName}'s pancreatic drainage referral?

answerChoices.label: Arrange magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
answerChoices.rationale: The new inflammatory collection does not classify the separate older tail lesion. Noninvasive duct/cyst mapping addresses the unresolved relation before an inflammatory drainage pathway is applied to that target.

answerChoices.label: Arrange endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
answerChoices.rationale: This approaches the lumen from downstream before the older cyst's relationship to it has been established; it is not the preferred initial noninvasive cyst/duct characterization.

answerChoices.label: Arrange repeat pancreatic computed tomography
answerChoices.rationale: CT has already characterized the new collection but has not resolved the older cyst's duct relationship. Repeating the same acquisition does not target that remaining question.

decisionNodes.explanation: Keep the two structures separate. A newly formed mature fluid collection after interstitial pancreatitis is not evidence that a pre-existing septated tail cyst has the same origin. Before the larger tail lesion is sent down a pseudocyst-drainage pathway, MRI/MRCP can map its relationship to the main duct and guide cyst-specific assessment. The observations neither prove cancer nor select a resection.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next study plan should guide disposition of {patientName}'s drainage referral?

answerChoices.label: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography for cyst assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Its presence years earlier prevents assigning a new inflammatory drainage pathway from the recent episode; define its identity and duct relation before planning puncture.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic ultrasonography for a transmural drainage window at A
answerChoices.rationale: This treats the disputed target identity as settled and moves to access planning before the pre-existing lesion has been evaluated as a cystic lesion.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic retrograde pancreatography for transpapillary access to A
answerChoices.rationale: An invasive access study does not resolve the prior question of whether A belongs on an inflammatory drainage pathway.

decisionNodes.explanation: Map the referral to the actual lesion before selecting a procedure. A is not the larger recent collection B: it predates the episode by years and is septated. Persistent symptoms after pancreatitis therefore cannot establish A as a pseudocyst to drain. MRI/MRCP is the best offered characterization study before disposition of that referral; it does not complete every neoplasm assessment, rule out later endoscopic evaluation or settle every subsequent lesion-specific treatment.

answerChoices.label: Increase the bedtime pancrelipase dose
answerChoices.rationale: More enzymes at a fasting time do not correct their separation from food.

answerChoices.label: Give prescribed pancrelipase during meals and snacks
answerChoices.rationale: The enzymes must accompany food; correct administration before judging adequacy of the regimen.

answerChoices.rationale: Acid suppression may help inadequate enzyme response, but does not replace administering enzymes with food.

decisionNodes.explanation: Pancrelipase taken at bedtime cannot reliably mix with food eaten earlier. Move the prescribed regimen to meals and snacks, then reassess stool and nutritional response. answerChoices.rationale: Repeated endoscopic attempts have not achieved durable relief; another identical cycle is less appropriate than surgery in this candidate.

answerChoices.rationale: A block may palliate selected patients but does not address the demonstrated obstructed duct after failed decompression.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After food-linked pancrelipase, stools improve and weight stabilizes. Disabling epigastric pain persists. Prior stone extraction and repeated pancreatic-duct stent exchanges gave only brief relief. answerChoices.label: Repeat ERCP with pancreatic-duct stenting
answerChoices.rationale: Repeated endoscopic attempts have not achieved durable relief; another identical cycle is less appropriate than surgery in this candidate.

answerChoices.label: Longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy
answerChoices.rationale: The dilated obstructed duct and repeated endoscopic failure support surgical drainage when there is no dominant head mass.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided celiac plexus block
answerChoices.rationale: A block may palliate selected patients but does not address the demonstrated obstructed duct after failed decompression.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next investigation should resolve {patientName}'s pancreatic lesion before systemic treatment is selected?

answerChoices.label: Pancreatic MRI with MRCP
answerChoices.rationale: MRI can clarify an imaging differential but does not repair the tissue confirmation needed before contemplated systemic treatment when the first sample missed the target.

answerChoices.label: Repeat EUS-guided core sampling of the head lesion
answerChoices.rationale: The initial sample did not represent the lesion. Repeat targeted tissue acquisition is required to resolve persistent suspicion before systemic therapy.

answerChoices.label: ERCP with biliary brush cytology
answerChoices.rationale: Biliary brushings sample a different target and are less suitable than direct EUS sampling of this solid pancreatic lesion for the tissue question.

decisionNodes.explanation: Fibrosis and acini from beside a new mass do not exclude malignancy within it. Persistent clinical and imaging suspicion plus the plan for possible systemic therapy require representative tissue. Repeat EUS-guided sampling addresses the actual missed target; another image or biliary brushing does not supply equivalent confirmation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s pancreatic-head cancer findings?

answerChoices.label: Pancreaticoduodenectomy with venous reconstruction now
answerChoices.rationale: Venous resection may ultimately be feasible, but this borderline anatomy favors neoadjuvant systemic treatment and reassessment first.

answerChoices.label: Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy followed by restaging
answerChoices.rationale: Potentially reconstructible venous involvement supports a borderline pathway with systemic therapy and reassessment rather than immediate surgery or permanent exclusion.

answerChoices.label: Palliative systemic chemotherapy with no resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Venous involvement alone, with reconstructible segments and no distant disease, does not establish permanent unresectability.

decisionNodes.explanation: The venous pattern raises a borderline resection problem; patent segments preserve the possibility of reconstruction. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy with restaging is the preferred offered sequence. It does not guarantee later resection and does not impose the same sequence on every clearly resectable pancreatic cancer.
sourceLabels: Multidisciplinary consensus on pancreatic cancer management

decisionNodes.stem: Which biliary drainage strategy should precede {patientName}'s planned neoadjuvant treatment?

answerChoices.label: ERCP with a plastic biliary stent
answerChoices.rationale: Plastic stenting drains the duct but is less durable than metal stenting during the planned treatment interval.

answerChoices.label: Surgical biliary bypass
answerChoices.rationale: An operative bypass is more invasive than standard endoscopic drainage when the papilla is accessible.

answerChoices.label: ERCP with a covered metal biliary stent
answerChoices.rationale: Endoscopic covered metal drainage is the verified preferred strategy for obstructive jaundice before neoadjuvant treatment.

decisionNodes.explanation: This is obstructive jaundice before a planned systemic-treatment interval, a drainage indication even without cholangitis. With standard access, ERCP with a covered metal stent is preferred in the verified consensus. This does not support routine drainage of every jaundiced patient proceeding directly to early surgery.

decisionNodes.stem: Which biliary drainage strategy should precede {patientName}'s planned neoadjuvant treatment?

answerChoices.label: ERCP with a plastic biliary stent
answerChoices.rationale: Plastic stenting drains the duct but is less durable than metal stenting during the planned treatment interval.

answerChoices.label: Surgical biliary bypass
answerChoices.rationale: An operative bypass is more invasive than standard endoscopic drainage when the papilla is accessible.

answerChoices.label: ERCP with a covered metal biliary stent
answerChoices.rationale: Endoscopic covered metal drainage is the verified preferred strategy for obstructive jaundice before neoadjuvant treatment.

decisionNodes.explanation: This is obstructive jaundice before a planned systemic-treatment interval, a drainage indication even without cholangitis. With standard access, ERCP with a covered metal stent is preferred in the verified consensus. This does not support routine drainage of every jaundiced patient proceeding directly to early surgery.

authorGate.interpret: Identify malignant obstruction in a patient entering neoadjuvant therapy rather than immediate surgery.

answerChoices.label: Systemic therapy for metastatic pancreatic cancer
answerChoices.rationale: Representative distant disease changes the treatment pathway; pancreatic resection is not the usual curative strategy for metastatic adenocarcinoma.

answerChoices.label: Neoadjuvant therapy followed by distal-resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: A standard borderline-localized sequence does not fit newly confirmed multifocal distant disease.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A standard borderline-localized sequence does not fit newly confirmed multifocal distant disease.

answerChoices.label: Radiotherapy directed to the pancreatic primary
answerChoices.rationale: Local radiotherapy does not address newly confirmed multifocal distant disease as the initial overall strategy.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Local radiotherapy does not address newly confirmed multifocal distant disease as the initial overall strategy.

question.explanation: This is representative distant tissue, rather than an indeterminate scan or a regional node. The confirmed liver disease changes treatment intent toward systemic therapy. authorGate.interpret: Recognize that the new sample establishes distant pancreatic cancer spread, not a local staging detail.
authorGate.apply: Change initial treatment intent to systemic care.
authorGate.closestError: Apply the memorized tail-operation rule despite newly proven multifocal distant disease.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Targeted liver core is concordant metastatic adenocarcinoma; multiple hepatic lesions are present.
authorGate.consequence: Offer a major nonstandard operation without first addressing disseminated disease.
authorGate.counterfactual: Benign hepatic findings with borderline localized venous involvement would favor neoadjuvant therapy followed by resection reassessment.
authorGate.deletionTest: The completed biopsy, not a presumptive MRI, supplies the intent change. No microscopic marker panel is invented to claim pancreatic specificity.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial management plan is most appropriate for {patientName}'s pancreatic tumor?

answerChoices.label: Pancreatic tumor enucleation
answerChoices.rationale: Immediate intervention is not required for a carefully evaluated subcentimeter asymptomatic nonfunctioning lesion.

answerChoices.label: Structured pancreatic imaging surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Initial observation is acceptable for this selected low-risk nonfunctioning subcentimeter tumor with follow-up.

answerChoices.label: Distal pancreatectomy with regional node assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Formal resection adds pancreatic morbidity without a supplied high-risk finding that outweighs surveillance here.

decisionNodes.explanation: The tumor is small, nonfunctioning and without an adverse duct or staging finding. Structured surveillance is an accepted initial strategy; a NET label does not mandate immediate pancreatectomy. Follow-up remains active and must reassess new clinical or imaging changes.
sourceLabels: NANETS surgical management of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
NCI PDQ pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors treatment

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A later surveillance record shows the body lesion has grown to 2.8 cm. EUS places its deep margin 1 mm from the main duct, with new upstream dilation. Repeat staging shows no distant disease. The original small biopsy had a low proliferation index. Updated cardiopulmonary assessment supports pancreatic resection.
decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s pancreatic tumor now?

answerChoices.label: Continue pancreatic imaging surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Actual growth and new ductal effect override the previous low-risk surveillance premise.

answerChoices.label: Enucleation of the pancreatic body lesion
answerChoices.rationale: This larger deep lesion lies close to the main duct; enucleation risks duct injury and does not provide the same regional assessment.

answerChoices.label: Distal pancreatectomy with regional node assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Growth, larger size and duct proximity favor formal resection rather than continued observation or enucleation.

decisionNodes.explanation: The later tumor is no longer the lesion for which surveillance was selected. Growth and an upstream duct effect create a new management problem. Its deep margin is too close to the main duct for the favorable enucleation criteria; formal resection with regional assessment is the appropriate offered operation. A limited old sample cannot freeze future risk assessment.

authorGate.interpret: Combine size and function with staging and duct anatomy rather than classify by tumor name alone.
authorGate.apply: Choose active surveillance while avoiding unnecessary pancreatic morbidity.
authorGate.closestError: Choose enucleation simply because the lesion is small and localized.
authorGate.decidingObservation: 8-mm nonfunctioning grade-1 tumor, unchanged duct, no spread and available follow-up.
authorGate.consequence: Expose a selected low-risk patient to avoidable pancreatic surgery.
authorGate.counterfactual: A comparable small lesion causing a confirmed insulin-excess syndrome and separated from the duct could favor enucleation.
authorGate.deletionTest: Function, size, duct and follow-up define the observation boundary. Removing them permits a different intervention decision. No numerical cancer probability is invented.
authorGate.cueAttack: No 'indolent' conclusion or refusal of surgery is supplied. All options are concrete lesion-directed plans. Surveillance is a specific continuing action with wait metadata, not a generic shared-decision phrase.
authorGate.stageCategory: One initial plan for an already characterized localized tumor.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate prediction: distinguish selected low-risk observation from automatic excision of all neuroendocrine lesions.
authorGate.singleBest: Surveillance is acceptable and preferred among these plans for this exact profile. A universal rule for 1-2 cm tumors is withheld.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next investigation should guide {patientName}'s pancreatic operation?

answerChoices.label: Somatostatin-receptor PET/CT
answerChoices.rationale: Receptor imaging can stage NETs, but does not resolve the local lesion-to-duct relationship needed for this operative choice.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic ultrasound of the pancreatic lesion
answerChoices.rationale: EUS adds local anatomic detail when the relationship to the main duct can alter the operation.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic retrograde pancreatography
answerChoices.rationale: Duct opacification is not the preferred way to characterize the small solid lesion's anatomic relation when EUS can address it.

decisionNodes.explanation: The hormone diagnosis and systemic staging are already established. The remaining question is local anatomy that can change the operation. EUS can define that relationship; a receptor scan or invasive pancreatogram does not supply equivalent operative detail for this problem.

decisionNodes.stem: Which pancreatic operation should be recommended for {patientName}'s localized lesion?

answerChoices.label: Central pancreatectomy with reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: Central resection is an alternative for a deep neck lesion that cannot be enucleated; the current superficial lesion has favorable duct separation.

answerChoices.label: Enucleation with intraoperative ultrasound
answerChoices.rationale: A small localized functional lesion sufficiently separated from the main duct is suited to a limited operation with intraoperative anatomic confirmation.

answerChoices.label: Distal pancreatectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Removing the distal gland is more extensive than needed for a superficial neck lesion that can be enucleated.

decisionNodes.explanation: The lesion is solitary, small, superficial and separated from the main duct, without invasive findings. Enucleation with intraoperative ultrasound is the appropriate offered operation for this localized insulinoma. Functioning symptoms support treatment despite small size; this is different from surveillance of the prior nonfunctioning NET case.

authorGate.closestError: Apply an invasive-cancer positive-margin rule to low-grade IPMN.

authorGate.consequence: Unnecessary total gland loss or loss of appropriate follow-up.
authorGate.counterfactual: A high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma margin would make further resection a serious option; a completely removed noninvasive MCN could instead support discharge from pancreatic surveillance.
authorGate.deletionTest: Margin grade and histologic cyst type separately determine the two incorrect plans; neither can be deleted. Fitness establishes a potential benefit from follow-up without specifying an arbitrary interval.

caseComposition.sequenceAudit: First feedback explains modality selection without teaching high-risk measurements or surgery. The later pancreatic MRI is an existing returned record, not a result produced by this sidecar. Its nodule and duct findings introduce the management decision.

Node one scores target/chronology characterization; its feedback does not name a later operation. Node two adds completed EUS assessment, symptom attribution and a different care phase. B is unscored background; acute collection drainage remains the other topic's scope.
Standalone. Morphology must be interpreted together with objective compression; no prior diagnosis or feedback supplies a treatment.

The first node concerns failed drug-food delivery, not pain. The second supplies actual nutritional response plus a separate persistent obstructive pain history. First feedback does not name surgical options or endoscopic failure criteria.
Standalone specimen-target adequacy decision. No inference about autoimmune pancreatitis or a steroid regimen is scored.

First node scores borderline venous anatomy and treatment sequence. Its explanation does not discuss jaundice, drainage or stent type. Second node supplies new laboratory/symptom data during an established neoadjuvant plan.

First decision resolves an uncertain distant site; first feedback does not state a metastatic treatment key. Later MRI and biopsy are completed outside records. The second decision concerns changed treatment intent, not the frozen distal-operation association.

First node addresses initial low-risk surveillance. Second node is a later outside follow-up record with real growth and changed duct anatomy. Initial feedback avoids a larger-tumor threshold or resection/enucleation rule.

The endocrine syndrome is supplied and outside this lane's scoring. First feedback requests anatomic planning without stating the later operation or duct-distance criterion. The returned EUS record earns a separate operation decision.

decisionNodes.stem: Which disposition of {patientName}'s procedure referral for lesion A is best supported by the dated images?

answerChoices.label: Redirect A to EUS characterization and selective sampling
answerChoices.rationale: A existed before the first attack and has enlarged. The referral should evaluate a pancreatic cyst before therapeutic drainage; EUS can address the remaining management-relevant uncertainty.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with transgastric catheter drainage of A
answerChoices.rationale: This treats A as the new post-inflammatory collection even though that chronology belongs to B. Gastric proximity does not establish the disease being drained.

answerChoices.label: Redirect A to percutaneous catheter drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Changing the access route does not resolve the target's identity. The older enlarging cyst needs characterization rather than an assumed inflammatory drainage pathway.

decisionNodes.explanation: A was present before the first attack; B appeared afterward. That does not prove A is neoplastic, but it prevents attributing A's origin to this attack. Redirect the named therapeutic referral to cyst characterization. EUS is reasonable for this enlarged symptomatic cyst; MRI/MRCP can also contribute, and this question does not rank those two studies against each other.
sourceLabels: ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Pancreatic Cysts
Pancreatic cystic lesions: SIRM-AISP position paper

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Subsequent MRI and EUS show A as a 4.6-cm septated body-tail cyst without duct communication. It indents the stomach; endoscopy shows intact mucosa over the indentation. Meal-related fullness continues after B has resolved. Fluid CEA is markedly elevated; cytology contains scant mucinous epithelium without identified high-grade atypia. She has no major operative comorbidity.
decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s lesion A after this assessment?

answerChoices.label: Continue MRI surveillance of lesion A
answerChoices.rationale: Scant cytology without high-grade atypia cannot establish low whole-lesion risk. The large lesion and persistent compressive symptoms favor surgical evaluation.

answerChoices.label: Refer A for distal pancreatic resection
answerChoices.rationale: The morphology supports presumed MCN, and size plus persistent gastric compression support resection consideration in a fit patient without requiring proof of cancer.

answerChoices.label: Repeat EUS sampling of lesion A
answerChoices.rationale: Another sample may add information but a negative result would not remove the current size and symptom indications for surgical evaluation. Demonstrating invasive cancer is not a prerequisite for referral.

decisionNodes.explanation: The combined location, lack of duct communication and mucinous fluid assessment favor presumed MCN rather than establish its histology. A's size and persistent gastric compression support resection evaluation. CEA does not diagnose invasive cancer, and scant bland cells do not establish safety. Repeat sampling need not delay referral when the decision already rests on size and symptoms.
sourceLabels: ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Pancreatic Cysts

decisionNodes.stem: Which first management change best addresses {patientName}'s persistent malabsorption on this regimen?

answerChoices.label: Give intact granules in applesauce with food
answerChoices.rationale: The meal timing and prescribed amount are being followed, but crushing damages the granules' enteric protection. For this formulation, opening capsules onto acidic soft food while leaving the granules intact addresses the observed problem.

answerChoices.label: Increase pancrelipase amounts with meals and snacks
answerChoices.rationale: A larger amount taken with the same damaging preparation does not first correct the demonstrated delivery problem. The record does not establish that the prescribed amount is inadequate when properly administered.

answerChoices.label: Add acid suppression to the current enzyme regimen
answerChoices.rationale: Acid suppression can help selected incomplete responders, but administration should first preserve the intended delayed-release delivery. It does not make crushing the prescribed granules appropriate.

decisionNodes.explanation: Food timing is correct in this record. Crushing the delayed-release granules undermines their enteric protection. PANCREAZE capsules may be opened for someone who cannot swallow them, but the entire contents should be taken promptly in acidic soft food such as applesauce without crushing or chewing. Correct that preparation before deciding whether the prescribed amount or acid suppression needs adjustment. A response is not guaranteed; persistent symptoms still require reassessment.

decisionNodes.stem: Which tissue-acquisition strategy should next guide {patientName}'s treatment planning?

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided core sampling of the pancreatic lesion
answerChoices.rationale: The sampled neck tissue does not adequately represent the new uncinate/head target. Repeat targeted EUS tissue acquisition is preferred to percutaneous puncture of a pancreatic primary when confirmation is needed.

answerChoices.label: CT-guided core sampling of the pancreatic lesion
answerChoices.rationale: This could yield tissue, but EUS is the preferred route for the pancreatic primary in the supplied potentially treatable setting. A nondiagnostic first EUS sample from another site does not establish failure of correctly targeted EUS.

answerChoices.label: ERCP brush sampling of the distal bile-duct stricture
answerChoices.rationale: The distal stricture is a real alternative sampling target, but targeted pancreatic EUS sampling more directly addresses the solid primary and its prior inadequate sample. ERCP may separately be needed for drainage.

decisionNodes.explanation: The negative specimen came from the pancreatic neck, while the new suspicious target is in the uncinate/head. It therefore does not exclude malignancy in that target. Tissue confirmation is needed for the proposed systemic-treatment pathway. Repeat representative EUS acquisition is preferred to percutaneous puncture of the pancreatic primary; duct brushings are an alternative source of information, rather than a substitute for an adequate primary-lesion sample here.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s pancreatic-head cancer findings?

answerChoices.label: Upfront resection with venous reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: This potentially reconstructable venous pattern is not a simple clearly resectable relationship. Neoadjuvant therapy and reassessment are generally favored over proceeding directly to a technically complex operation.

answerChoices.label: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with surgical reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The venous abnormality with preserved adjacent segments and separated arteries supports a potentially reconstructable borderline pattern. Begin systemic treatment, then reassess staging and technical resectability.

answerChoices.label: Palliative chemotherapy with response assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Venous involvement alone does not establish permanent unresectability. The supplied negative distant staging and potentially reconstructable local pattern retain a possible resection pathway.

decisionNodes.explanation: The venous contour change and short narrowed segment suggest borderline local anatomy rather than either a clear surgery-first relationship or necessarily permanent unresectability. Neoadjuvant systemic treatment with restaging and surgical reassessment is the best offered sequence. Patency above and below supports consideration of reconstruction; it does not guarantee technical feasibility, which requires specialist review.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The multidisciplinary team plans several cycles of preoperative chemotherapy for the pancreatic-head adenocarcinoma. Before treatment begins, pruritus and jaundice increase. Imaging shows intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile-duct dilation above the distal stricture. There is no fever or circulatory instability, and he has an unaltered upper gastrointestinal anatomy.
decisionNodes.stem: Which pre-treatment management plan is best for {patientName} at this visit?

answerChoices.label: ERCP metal stenting before chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Obstructive jaundice should be relieved before the planned neoadjuvant course. A self-expanding metal stent offers more durable drainage through that treatment interval than a plastic stent.

answerChoices.label: ERCP plastic stenting before chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Plastic stenting can decompress the duct but is more prone to occlusion during a prolonged neoadjuvant interval. The planned course makes durable metal-stent drainage preferable here.

answerChoices.label: Begin chemotherapy with bilirubin reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The patient has progressive obstructive jaundice before a multi-cycle course. Reassessment alone does not first relieve the obstruction or provide durable drainage.

decisionNodes.explanation: Progressive jaundice with upstream dilation represents clinically important biliary obstruction even without cholangitis. Drain it before the planned neoadjuvant course. Endoscopic self-expanding metal stenting is preferred to plastic stenting for durable drainage through that interval. This comparison does not establish one metal-stent design as universally best and does not create a numerical bilirubin rule.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial investigation should characterize the hepatic focus before {patientName}'s pancreatic operation is planned?

answerChoices.label: Dynamic contrast and diffusion-weighted liver MRI
answerChoices.rationale: Dedicated MRI can characterize the small indeterminate hepatic focus. Local pancreatic vessel clearance does not settle distant staging, and an unclassified focus should not automatically be called metastatic.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET/CT with liver assessment
answerChoices.rationale: This may supplement cancer staging, but the immediate problem is characterizing a very small unclassified focus. Dedicated liver MRI more directly addresses that question; PET findings would still need anatomic correlation.

answerChoices.label: CT-guided core sampling of the hepatic focus
answerChoices.rationale: Representative tissue would establish the nature of a suspicious focus, but attempting a core of this tiny not-yet-characterized target is not the preferred first characterization step. MRI can clarify whether sampling is needed and provide a better target.

decisionNodes.explanation: Absence of vascular contact describes local anatomy, not the nature of the liver focus. Characterize that focus before fixing an operative pathway. Dedicated liver MRI is a useful initial study for small indeterminate hepatic lesions; PET/CT can supplement staging, and biopsy can resolve a persisting suspicious target. None of those roles makes this unclassified CT focus a metastatic diagnosis.
sourceLabels: Multidisciplinary consensus on pancreatic cancer management
NCI PDQ pancreatic cancer treatment, health professional version

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Liver MRI shows three separated solid foci. A core from the largest contains malignant glands within hepatic tissue. Side-by-side pathology review finds the same gland morphology as in the pancreatic-tail core. No systemic treatment has been given; she remains independent in daily activities.
decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment strategy should be recommended for {patientName} after these liver findings?

answerChoices.label: Systemic chemotherapy with disease-control intent
answerChoices.rationale: The hepatic specimen contains tumor matching the pancreatic primary, establishing distant spread. Initial systemic treatment is appropriate; favorable local anatomy does not retain the same surgery-first curative pathway.

answerChoices.label: Preoperative chemotherapy with distal-resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: This uses the nonmetastatic preoperative framework. The liver tissue changes the initial treatment intent, even though systemic drugs may overlap and selected later local strategies can be discussed after response.

answerChoices.label: Upfront distal pancreatectomy with adjuvant chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: A technically removable primary is not sufficient for an upfront curative operation when distant tumor has been sampled. Initial systemic treatment addresses the established disease distribution.

decisionNodes.explanation: Malignant glands matching the pancreatic tumor are present in liver tissue, establishing distant pancreatic-cancer spread. That changes initial intent from a routine preoperative or surgery-first pathway to systemic disease control. It does not prohibit every later local treatment in a highly selected responding patient; it determines the starting strategy for this untreated presentation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial management plan is most appropriate for {patientName}'s pancreatic tumor?

answerChoices.label: Pancreatic tumor enucleation
answerChoices.rationale: Immediate intervention is not required for a carefully evaluated subcentimeter asymptomatic nonfunctioning lesion.

answerChoices.label: Structured pancreatic imaging surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Initial observation is acceptable for this selected low-risk nonfunctioning subcentimeter tumor with follow-up.

answerChoices.label: Distal pancreatectomy with regional node assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Formal resection adds pancreatic morbidity without a supplied high-risk finding that outweighs surveillance here.

decisionNodes.explanation: The sample has a lower-proliferation well-differentiated phenotype, and the small lesion has neither a functional syndrome nor duct obstruction or spread. Structured surveillance is an acceptable initial strategy for this selected subcentimeter nonfunctioning NET. Tissue sampling may underestimate whole-tumor grade, so surveillance is active reassessment rather than a declaration of benignity. A functioning syndrome, growth or obstructive change would require a different assessment.

decisionNodes.stem: Which additional investigation best addresses the remaining question before {patientName}'s pancreatic operation is selected?

answerChoices.label: Arterial calcium stimulation with hepatic venous insulin sampling
answerChoices.rationale: Two anatomic NETs do not identify the source of insulin excess. Selective calcium stimulation with venous sampling can add regional functional information in this setting.

answerChoices.label: Repeat EUS core sampling of the larger pancreatic nodule
answerChoices.rationale: Another conventional histologic core may characterize the larger tumor, but size and NET histology alone do not establish that it produces the insulin syndrome. Both nodules already have representative NET samples.

answerChoices.label: Somatostatin-receptor PET/CT of the pancreatic nodules
answerChoices.rationale: This can identify receptor-positive neuroendocrine tissue and aid staging, but receptor uptake alone does not establish which of these already identified NETs drives insulin secretion. A secretion-linked regional test more directly answers this question.

decisionNodes.explanation: In MEN1, more than one pancreatic NET may coexist, and the largest detected nodule need not be the cause of insulin excess. Conventional NET histology or somatostatin-receptor uptake does not by itself settle that functional assignment. Selective arterial calcium stimulation with hepatic venous insulin sampling can provide regional secretion information for specialist planning. Perfusion overlap limits precision; this does not choose an operation or establish superiority over every available functional tracer.

decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan should have been recommended for {patientName} at this point in the hospital course?

answerChoices.label: Antibiotics plus image-guided catheter drainage
answerChoices.rationale: The existing catheter drains a different collapsed compartment. Persistent infection with a separate collection needs effective source control; image-guided access is the less invasive initial approach in this stable record.

answerChoices.label: Antibiotics plus interval imaging reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The record contains ongoing infection with a separate undrained collection. The presence of an existing catheter does not establish source control when its side holes are confined to another compartment.

answerChoices.label: Antibiotics plus operative washout and drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Operative source control is a real option, but stable physiology without generalized peritonitis and an available image-guided approach favor a minimally invasive attempt first. This is not a requirement to delay surgery if the situation changes.

decisionNodes.explanation: The catheter's side holes are in the collapsed anterior space, while the infected-appearing collection occupies a separate posterior compartment. Antibiotics and the existing catheter have therefore not established adequate source control. Image-guided catheter drainage is the preferred initial addition in this stable hospital record. IR must choose new placement or exchange from the actual anatomy; the question does not promise that repositioning through the old tract will work. Operative drainage remains appropriate if interventional control fails or surgical indications develop.

decisionNodes.stem: Which pancreatic-remnant management plan should be recommended for {patientName} now?

answerChoices.label: Completion pancreatectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Low-grade margin dysplasia and an unconcerning remnant cyst do not establish a need to remove the remaining pancreas.

answerChoices.label: MRI-based surveillance of the pancreatic remnant
answerChoices.rationale: Resected IPMN still warrants remnant surveillance; the low-grade margin and low-risk remnant do not by themselves select completion surgery.

answerChoices.label: Discharge from pancreatic imaging follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The absence of invasive cancer does not remove the remnant risk associated with IPMN.

decisionNodes.explanation: Low-grade IPMN at a margin is not equivalent to invasive cancer at a margin. decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s lesion A after this assessment?

answerChoices.label: Continue MRI surveillance of lesion A
answerChoices.rationale: Scant cytology without high-grade atypia cannot establish low whole-lesion risk. The large lesion and persistent compressive symptoms favor surgical evaluation.

answerChoices.label: Refer A for distal pancreatic resection
answerChoices.rationale: The morphology supports presumed MCN, and size plus persistent gastric compression support resection consideration in a fit patient without requiring proof of cancer.

answerChoices.label: Repeat EUS sampling of lesion A
answerChoices.rationale: Another sample may add information but a negative result would not remove the current size and symptom indications for surgical evaluation. Demonstrating invasive cancer is not a prerequisite for referral.

decisionNodes.explanation: The combined location, lack of duct communication and mucinous fluid assessment favor presumed MCN rather than establish its histology. A's size and persistent gastric compression support resection evaluation. CEA does not diagnose invasive cancer, and scant bland cells do not establish safety. Repeat sampling need not delay referral when the decision already rests on size and symptoms.

decisionNodes.stem: Which first management change best addresses {patientName}'s persistent malabsorption on this regimen?

answerChoices.label: Give intact granules in applesauce with food
answerChoices.rationale: The meal timing and prescribed amount are being followed, but crushing damages the granules' enteric protection. For this formulation, opening capsules onto acidic soft food while leaving the granules intact addresses the observed problem.

answerChoices.label: Increase pancrelipase amounts with meals and snacks
answerChoices.rationale: A larger amount taken with the same damaging preparation does not first correct the demonstrated delivery problem. The record does not establish that the prescribed amount is inadequate when properly administered.

answerChoices.label: Add acid suppression to the current enzyme regimen
answerChoices.rationale: Acid suppression can help selected incomplete responders, but administration should first preserve the intended delayed-release delivery. It does not make crushing the prescribed granules appropriate.

decisionNodes.explanation: Food timing is correct in this record. Crushing the delayed-release granules undermines their enteric protection. PANCREAZE capsules may be opened for someone who cannot swallow them, but the entire contents should be taken promptly in acidic soft food such as applesauce without crushing or chewing. Correct that preparation before deciding whether the prescribed amount or acid suppression needs adjustment. A response is not guaranteed; persistent symptoms still require reassessment.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s pancreatic-head cancer findings?

answerChoices.label: Pancreaticoduodenectomy with venous reconstruction now
answerChoices.rationale: Venous resection may ultimately be feasible, but this borderline anatomy favors neoadjuvant systemic treatment and reassessment first.

answerChoices.label: Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy followed by restaging
answerChoices.rationale: Potentially reconstructible venous involvement supports a borderline pathway with systemic therapy and reassessment rather than immediate surgery or permanent exclusion.

answerChoices.label: Palliative systemic chemotherapy with no resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Venous involvement alone, with reconstructible segments and no distant disease, does not establish permanent unresectability.

case.learningSummary: The venous contour change and short narrowed segment suggest borderline local anatomy rather than either a clear surgery-first relationship or necessarily permanent unresectability. Neoadjuvant systemic treatment with restaging and surgical reassessment is the best offered sequence. Progressive jaundice with upstream dilation represents clinically important biliary obstruction even without cholangitis. Drain it before the planned neoadjuvant course. decisionNodes.stem: Which initial investigation should characterize the hepatic focus before {patientName}'s pancreatic operation is planned?

answerChoices.label: Dynamic contrast and diffusion-weighted liver MRI
answerChoices.rationale: Dedicated MRI can characterize the small indeterminate hepatic focus. Local pancreatic vessel clearance does not settle distant staging, and an unclassified focus should not automatically be called metastatic.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET/CT with liver assessment
answerChoices.rationale: This may supplement cancer staging, but the immediate problem is characterizing a very small unclassified focus. Dedicated liver MRI more directly addresses that question; PET findings would still need anatomic correlation.

answerChoices.label: CT-guided core sampling of the hepatic focus
answerChoices.rationale: Representative tissue would establish the nature of a suspicious focus, but attempting a core of this tiny not-yet-characterized target is not the preferred first characterization step. MRI can clarify whether sampling is needed and provide a better target.

decisionNodes.explanation: Absence of vascular contact describes local anatomy, not the nature of the liver focus. Characterize that focus before fixing an operative pathway. Dedicated liver MRI is a useful initial study for small indeterminate hepatic lesions; PET/CT can supplement staging, and biopsy can resolve a persisting suspicious target. None of those roles makes this unclassified CT focus a metastatic diagnosis.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial treatment strategy should be recommended for {patientName} after these liver findings?

answerChoices.label: Systemic chemotherapy with disease-control intent
answerChoices.rationale: The hepatic specimen contains tumor matching the pancreatic primary, establishing distant spread. Initial systemic treatment is appropriate; favorable local anatomy does not retain the same surgery-first curative pathway.

answerChoices.label: Preoperative chemotherapy with distal-resection reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: This uses the nonmetastatic preoperative framework. The liver tissue changes the initial treatment intent, even though systemic drugs may overlap and selected later local strategies can be discussed after response.

answerChoices.label: Upfront distal pancreatectomy with adjuvant chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: A technically removable primary is not sufficient for an upfront curative operation when distant tumor has been sampled. Initial systemic treatment addresses the established disease distribution.

decisionNodes.explanation: Malignant glands matching the pancreatic tumor are present in liver tissue, establishing distant pancreatic-cancer spread. That changes initial intent from a routine preoperative or surgery-first pathway to systemic disease control. It does not prohibit every later local treatment in a highly selected responding patient; it determines the starting strategy for this untreated presentation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which additional investigation best addresses the remaining question before {patientName}'s pancreatic operation is selected?

answerChoices.label: Arterial calcium stimulation with hepatic venous insulin sampling
answerChoices.rationale: Two anatomic NETs do not identify the source of insulin excess. Selective calcium stimulation with venous sampling can add regional functional information in this setting.

answerChoices.label: Repeat EUS core sampling of the larger pancreatic nodule
answerChoices.rationale: Another conventional histologic core may characterize the larger tumor, but size and NET histology alone do not establish that it produces the insulin syndrome. Both nodules already have representative NET samples.

answerChoices.label: Somatostatin-receptor PET/CT of the pancreatic nodules
answerChoices.rationale: This can identify receptor-positive neuroendocrine tissue and aid staging, but receptor uptake alone does not establish which of these already identified NETs drives insulin secretion. A secretion-linked regional test more directly answers this question.

decisionNodes.explanation: In MEN1, more than one pancreatic NET may coexist, and the largest detected nodule need not be the cause of insulin excess. Conventional NET histology or somatostatin-receptor uptake does not by itself settle that functional assignment. Selective arterial calcium stimulation with hepatic venous insulin sampling can provide regional secretion information for specialist planning. Perfusion overlap limits precision; this does not choose an operation or establish superiority over every available functional tracer.

authorGate.interpret: Recognize that concordant CT/MRI/EUS detection of two histologic NETs leaves the symptom-producing region unassigned; tumor size is not a functional result.
authorGate.apply: Select a secretion-linked regionalization investigation rather than another conventional tissue sample or receptor-distribution study.
authorGate.closestError: Repeat sampling of the larger tumor on the assumption that size determines which lesion causes hypoglycemia.
authorGate.decidingObservation: There are two anatomically confirmed NETs but one established insulin-excess syndrome, with no result linking secretion to either focus.
authorGate.consequence: An operation could target a nonfunctioning nodule while leaving the hormonal source unaddressed.
authorGate.counterfactual: If the remaining uncertainty were whether the larger focus was actually NET tissue because its first sample was inadequate, repeat EUS core sampling could become appropriate.
authorGate.deletionTest: A single confidently localized functional target would remove the multiple-lesion assignment problem. Without established insulin excess, invasive secretion regionalization would not be justified by incidental nodules alone.
authorGate.cueAttack: Replaced the explicitly unresolved duct-distance recall item with raw competing-lesion findings. No availability permission selects the key, and no unrevealed duct gap is named as the task. All options are actual additional investigations.
authorGate.stageCategory: One additional investigation for functional assignment before operative planning.
authorGate.difficulty: Moderate-hard prediction: distinguish anatomic concordance and NET identity from hormone attribution, then choose a secretion-linked test.
authorGate.singleBest: Calcium stimulation most directly addresses functional regionalization among the offered tests. It is not a guarantee of a unique lesion, a rule for all insulinomas, or a comparison against GLP-1-receptor imaging.

resolution.clarity: The remaining operative question is functional assignment among two identified NETs, not a supplied missing duct measurement.
resolution.cues: Removed named duct-distance gap and access/availability permission. CT/MRI/EUS report two anatomic candidates without assigning secretion.
resolution.fairness: Known MEN1 and biochemically established insulin excess are supplied rather than tested in the endocrine topic. Calcium stimulation can add functional regionalization; it is not promised to name a unique tumor or outrank every tracer. No complete exclusion of metastasis is claimed.
resolution.suggestions: The new concept and fictional patient distinguish this objective from EUS operative-anatomy mapping. Conventional biopsy and receptor imaging are credible tests but do not by themselves assign insulin production.
resolution.outcome: Two-step moderate-hard new-meaning candidate supported by a CC BY technical review and independent series.

review.title: Local anatomic assessment before insulinoma surgery

cues.phrase: the study does not resolve its distance from the main duct
cues.why: The presentation explicitly names the unanswered operative-anatomy question. The learner is asked to recall the test that addresses it rather than discover what still needs to be established.

cues.phrase: endocrinology confirms a sporadic insulinoma syndrome
cues.why: The functional diagnosis has already been resolved; with a localized focus and no metastasis, the receptor-imaging option has little remaining purpose in this particular comparison. This is legitimate background, but it leaves a simple modality-choice task.

fairness: EUS is a defensible preferred offered investigation to define lesion/duct anatomy. Diagnostic pancreatography is not an equivalent routine method for characterizing the surrounding tumor, and receptor imaging does not supply the same operative detail.

The explanation's 'systemic staging are already established' is stronger than a brief negative CT summary needs to be. The key can be supported by the unresolved local question without suggesting that CT guarantees absence of all metastatic disease.
The later EUS update coherently answers the anatomic question. This node does not name enucleation, but its feedback deliberately focuses the next node on duct relationship.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the defect is mainly supplied interpretation and limited competition, not a wrong preferred test.
suggestions: Create a clinically supported conflict in localization or operative anatomy that changes which test is needed, with competing investigations at that same decision stage.
Alternatively retain as explicitly basic operative-imaging practice, rather than calling an already named gap plus a test choice two consequential steps.
Keep feedback limited to what the supplied staging shows rather than implying complete exclusion of metastatic disease.

review.title: Operation for a superficial localized insulinoma
fairness: The learner integrates functional disease requiring treatment with a small superficial lesion separated from the main duct, then selects limited excision rather than a segmental resection. The neck location makes central pancreatectomy a recognizable alternative that the favorable local anatomy defeats.
Enucleation with intraoperative ultrasound is the best offered operation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the supplied localization and operative principle.

The prior explanation identifies the importance of local anatomy but does not name the operation or supply the favorable distance. The update supplies the decisive observations and can be used with the shared presentation without remembering an earlier answer.

Options are actual operations with reasonably comparable specificity. 'With intraoperative ultrasound' adds a legitimate operative adjunct; it does not create a unique explanatory sentence or an answer-selecting convergence pattern.
The final sentence comparing a 'prior nonfunctioning NET case' is unnecessary cross-case teaching; all necessary facts for this node are present here, so it does not invalidate the decision.
suggestions: Optional feedback cleanup: remove the reference to a 'prior nonfunctioning NET case' or make the comparison generic, since a separately selected encounter need not have preceded this one.

review.title: Postoperative vomiting with inflammation and altered drain output
fairness: The learner must distinguish an isolated emptying problem from a secondary postoperative abdominal complication using the inflammatory course and abrupt drain-output change, then choose the appropriate anatomic investigation. The emptying study and MRCP represent different, plausible diagnostic targets.
Contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic CT is the best offered next investigation in the stable patient without generalized guarding. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The historical hospital-review frame is explicit, and the update supplies the symptoms and physiologic context. It does not ask the present outpatient clinic to perform urgent inpatient care.
The explanation does not disclose the subsequent collection or its catheter position. The next node introduces new source-control information. No nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At readmission, vomiting and abdominal fullness recur after initial oral intake. Temperature and white-cell count rise. Previously enzyme-rich drain output abruptly decreases. Blood pressure is maintained and there is no generalized guarding.
decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should have been obtained next in {patientName}'s outside-hospital record?

answerChoices.label: Radionuclide gastric-emptying study
answerChoices.rationale: A functional emptying test does not first address systemic inflammation and possible inadequately drained postoperative fluid.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis
answerChoices.rationale: Cross-sectional evaluation is needed to investigate a postoperative collection or other secondary complication.

answerChoices.label: Pancreatic MRI with MRCP
answerChoices.rationale: Duct mapping may later inform persistent leakage, but the immediate unresolved issue is a new inflammatory abdominal complication.

decisionNodes.explanation: Vomiting after pancreatic surgery should not be assigned to isolated delayed emptying while systemic inflammation and changing drain behavior suggest a secondary complication. CT is the appropriate offered initial assessment of the current abdomen. Duct mapping or functional testing addresses different remaining questions.
sourceLabels: Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for chronic pancreatitis 2021

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The hospital CT shows a rim-enhancing operative-bed collection. The drain tip lies outside the cavity. Antibiotics have begun, but fever continues. There is a percutaneous access route; no diffuse free air or generalized peritonitis is present, and circulation remains stable.
decisionNodes.stem: Which source-control procedure should be recommended in {patientName}'s hospital record now?

answerChoices.label: ERCP with transpapillary pancreatic stenting
answerChoices.rationale: A possible duct intervention does not drain the demonstrated infected cavity whose catheter is outside it.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided drain repositioning into the collection
answerChoices.rationale: Effective interventional drainage addresses the current accessible infected collection while antibiotics continue.

answerChoices.label: Laparotomy with operative drainage
answerChoices.rationale: An initial reoperation is more invasive than correcting accessible drainage in this stable patient without generalized contamination.

decisionNodes.explanation: The catheter does not drain the cavity shown on CT. Antibiotics need effective source control, and this stable record supports image-guided repositioning rather than immediate reoperation. A separate duct-directed treatment would require its own anatomic assessment; it is not a substitute for draining the current infected cavity.
sourceLabels: Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for chronic pancreatitis 2021

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Later in the same admission, fresh blood briefly appears in the drain and then stops. Hemoglobin falls. The collection had contained enzyme-rich fluid. There is no hematemesis or melena, and circulation is currently maintained.
decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should be obtained urgently in {patientName}'s hospital record after this bleeding episode?

answerChoices.label: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: The observed extraluminal drain bleeding favors evaluation of a postoperative vascular source rather than an initial mucosal examination.

answerChoices.label: MRI with MRCP of the pancreatic duct
answerChoices.rationale: Duct mapping does not identify and control an urgent arterial bleeding risk.

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the abdomen
answerChoices.rationale: A transient drain bleed after pancreatic surgery can be a sentinel event; urgent vascular imaging can direct endovascular treatment in a stable patient.

review.title: Transient postoperative drain bleeding and vascular investigation
fairness: The learner must interpret a stopped bleed with a hemoglobin fall in the setting of enzyme-rich postoperative fluid as potentially important vascular bleeding, then choose urgent vascular imaging for the currently stable patient. Cessation is the plausible reassurance trap.

CT angiography is the best offered investigation. The supplied extraluminal drain bleeding and lack of luminal symptoms make initial upper endoscopy less appropriate, while MRCP does not evaluate the urgent vascular concern.

The update restates the pancreatic-fluid context, bleeding evidence and current circulation, so it is sufficiently independent of the previous answer. Earlier feedback teaches drainage rather than sentinel bleeding.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. 'Later in the same admission' leaves the interval after surgery and drain manipulation imprecise; this does not defeat urgent evaluation with a hemoglobin fall, but timing would help distinguish delayed vascular erosion from immediate procedural trauma.
The negative gastrointestinal symptoms are legitimate localization evidence rather than wording that literally matches the CTA option.
suggestions: Optional chronology clarification: state the relationship of the bleed to surgery and the most recent drain manipulation using supported case observations; do not invent a universal timing cutoff.

review.title: Low-grade IPMN margin and pancreatic-remnant surveillance
fairness: The learner must interpret low-grade dysplasia at a margin differently from invasive or high-grade disease, then preserve remnant surveillance despite the absence of invasive carcinoma. Completion pancreatectomy and discharge represent distinct, recognizable over- and undertreatment errors.

Surveillance is the best offered plan for this fit patient with low-grade margin dysplasia and no concerning remnant imaging feature. The retained remnant cyst also makes discontinuing imaging a poor answer here.
The explanation appropriately distinguishes resected IPMN from completely resected noninvasive MCN and does not invent a surveillance interval or cancer probability.

The task is complete, options are parallel management strategies, and no preceding node is needed. No confident clinical inaccuracy or answer-selecting wording shortcut identified; exact surveillance-policy details still require clinician review.

record.title: Operation for a superficial localized insulinoma
fairness: The learner integrates functional disease requiring treatment with a small superficial lesion separated from the main duct, then selects limited excision rather than a segmental resection. The neck location makes central pancreatectomy a recognizable alternative that the favorable local anatomy defeats.
Enucleation with intraoperative ultrasound is the best offered operation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the supplied localization and operative principle.

The prior explanation identifies the importance of local anatomy but does not name the operation or supply the favorable distance. The update supplies the decisive observations and can be used with the shared presentation without remembering an earlier answer.

Options are actual operations with reasonably comparable specificity. 'With intraoperative ultrasound' adds a legitimate operative adjunct; it does not create a unique explanatory sentence or an answer-selecting convergence pattern.
The final sentence comparing a 'prior nonfunctioning NET case' is unnecessary cross-case teaching; all necessary facts for this node are present here, so it does not invalidate the decision.
suggestions: Optional feedback cleanup: remove the reference to a 'prior nonfunctioning NET case' or make the comparison generic, since a separately selected encounter need not have preceded this one.

answerChoices.rationale: Duct opacification is not the preferred way to characterize the small solid lesion's anatomic relation when EUS can address it.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: EUS shows a solitary 12-mm superficial focus in the pancreatic neck, 6 mm from the main duct. There are no suspicious nodes or local invasion. The endocrine team confirms that the lesion explains {patientName}'s documented hypoglycemia.
decisionNodes.stem: Which pancreatic operation should be recommended for {patientName}'s localized lesion?

answerChoices.label: Central pancreatectomy with reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: Central resection is an alternative for a deep neck lesion that cannot be enucleated; the current superficial lesion has favorable duct separation.

answerChoices.label: Enucleation with intraoperative ultrasound
answerChoices.rationale: A small localized functional lesion sufficiently separated from the main duct is suited to a limited operation with intraoperative anatomic confirmation.

answerChoices.label: Distal pancreatectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Removing the distal gland is more extensive than needed for a superficial neck lesion that can be enucleated.

decisionNodes.explanation: The lesion is solitary, small, superficial and separated from the main duct, without invasive findings. Enucleation with intraoperative ultrasound is the appropriate offered operation for this localized insulinoma. Functioning symptoms support treatment despite small size; this is different from surveillance of the prior nonfunctioning NET case.

decisionNodes.stem: Which disposition of {patientName}'s procedure referral for lesion A is best supported by the dated images?

answerChoices.label: Redirect A to EUS characterization and selective sampling
answerChoices.rationale: A existed before the first attack and has enlarged. The referral should evaluate a pancreatic cyst before therapeutic drainage; EUS can address the remaining management-relevant uncertainty.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with transgastric catheter drainage of A
answerChoices.rationale: This treats A as the new post-inflammatory collection even though that chronology belongs to B. Gastric proximity does not establish the disease being drained.

answerChoices.label: Redirect A to percutaneous catheter drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Changing the access route does not resolve the target's identity. The older enlarging cyst needs characterization rather than an assumed inflammatory drainage pathway.

decisionNodes.explanation: A was present before the first attack; B appeared afterward. That does not prove A is neoplastic, but it prevents attributing A's origin to this attack. Redirect the named therapeutic referral to cyst characterization. EUS is reasonable for this enlarged symptomatic cyst; MRI/MRCP can also contribute, and this question does not rank those two studies against each other.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Subsequent MRI and EUS show A as a 4.6-cm septated body-tail cyst without duct communication. It indents the stomach; endoscopy shows intact mucosa over the indentation. Meal-related fullness continues after B has resolved. Fluid CEA is markedly elevated; cytology contains scant mucinous epithelium without identified high-grade atypia. She has no major operative comorbidity.
decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s lesion A after this assessment?

answerChoices.label: Continue MRI surveillance of lesion A
answerChoices.rationale: Scant cytology without high-grade atypia cannot establish low whole-lesion risk. The large lesion and persistent compressive symptoms favor surgical evaluation.

answerChoices.label: Refer A for distal pancreatic resection
answerChoices.rationale: The morphology supports presumed MCN, and size plus persistent gastric compression support resection consideration in a fit patient without requiring proof of cancer.

answerChoices.label: Repeat EUS sampling of lesion A
answerChoices.rationale: Another sample may add information but a negative result would not remove the current size and symptom indications for surgical evaluation. Demonstrating invasive cancer is not a prerequisite for referral.

decisionNodes.explanation: The combined location, lack of duct communication and mucinous fluid assessment favor presumed MCN rather than establish its histology. A's size and persistent gastric compression support resection evaluation. CEA does not diagnose invasive cancer, and scant bland cells do not establish safety. Repeat sampling need not delay referral when the decision already rests on size and symptoms.

case.learningSummary: A was present before the first attack; B appeared afterward. That does not prove A is neoplastic, but it prevents attributing A's origin to this attack. Redirect the named therapeutic referral to cyst characterization. EUS is reasonable for this enlarged symptomatic cyst; MRI/MRCP can also contribute, and this question does not rank those two studies against each other. The combined location, lack of duct communication and mucinous fluid assessment favor presumed MCN rather than establish its histology. A's size and persistent gastric compression support resection evaluation. CEA does not diagnose invasive cancer, and scant bland cells do not establish safety. Repeat sampling need not delay referral when the decision already rests on size and symptoms.

She has no major operative comorbidity.

record.title: Growing pancreatic NET with duct proximity and dilation
fairness: Growth to the current tumor size and a new upstream duct effect require reconsidering surveillance; deep duct proximity then distinguishes enucleation from formal resection. These are two consequential decisions with plausible errors.

Distal pancreatectomy with regional node assessment is the best offered plan for this body lesion, given the current findings and operative fitness. The old low-grade sample does not negate subsequent structural progression.

The exact surveillance interval is not needed to rank these choices because current size and duct effects independently matter; it would be needed if the task were calculating a growth-rate criterion.

The update restates the current tumor, anatomy, staging and operative fitness. Prior feedback encourages reassessment but does not supply the enucleation-versus-resection discriminator. No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical answer shortcut identified.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial management plan is most appropriate for {patientName}'s pancreatic tumor?

answerChoices.label: Pancreatic tumor enucleation
answerChoices.rationale: Immediate intervention is not required for a carefully evaluated subcentimeter asymptomatic nonfunctioning lesion.

answerChoices.label: Structured pancreatic imaging surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Initial observation is acceptable for this selected low-risk nonfunctioning subcentimeter tumor with follow-up.

answerChoices.label: Distal pancreatectomy with regional node assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Formal resection adds pancreatic morbidity without a supplied high-risk finding that outweighs surveillance here.

decisionNodes.explanation: The tumor is small, nonfunctioning and without an adverse duct or staging finding. Structured surveillance is an accepted initial strategy; a NET label does not mandate immediate pancreatectomy. Follow-up remains active and must reassess new clinical or imaging changes.
sourceLabels: NANETS surgical management of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
NCI PDQ pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors treatment

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A later surveillance record shows the body lesion has grown to 2.8 cm. EUS places its deep margin 1 mm from the main duct, with new upstream dilation. Repeat staging shows no distant disease. The original small biopsy had a low proliferation index. Updated cardiopulmonary assessment supports pancreatic resection.
decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s pancreatic tumor now?

answerChoices.label: Continue pancreatic imaging surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Actual growth and new ductal effect override the previous low-risk surveillance premise.

answerChoices.label: Enucleation of the pancreatic body lesion
answerChoices.rationale: This larger deep lesion lies close to the main duct; enucleation risks duct injury and does not provide the same regional assessment.

answerChoices.label: Distal pancreatectomy with regional node assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Growth, larger size and duct proximity favor formal resection rather than continued observation or enucleation.

decisionNodes.explanation: The later tumor is no longer the lesion for which surveillance was selected. Growth and an upstream duct effect create a new management problem. Its deep margin is too close to the main duct for the favorable enucleation criteria; formal resection with regional assessment is the appropriate offered operation. A limited old sample cannot freeze future risk assessment.
