record.title: Transient postoperative drain bleeding and vascular investigation
fairness: The learner must interpret a stopped bleed with a hemoglobin fall in the setting of enzyme-rich postoperative fluid as potentially important vascular bleeding, then choose urgent vascular imaging for the currently stable patient. Cessation is the plausible reassurance trap.

CT angiography is the best offered investigation. The supplied extraluminal drain bleeding and lack of luminal symptoms make initial upper endoscopy less appropriate, while MRCP does not evaluate the urgent vascular concern.

The update restates the pancreatic-fluid context, bleeding evidence and current circulation, so it is sufficiently independent of the previous answer. Earlier feedback teaches drainage rather than sentinel bleeding.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. 'Later in the same admission' leaves the interval after surgery and drain manipulation imprecise; this does not defeat urgent evaluation with a hemoglobin fall, but timing would help distinguish delayed vascular erosion from immediate procedural trauma.
The negative gastrointestinal symptoms are legitimate localization evidence rather than wording that literally matches the CTA option.
suggestions: Optional chronology clarification: state the relationship of the bleed to surgery and the most recent drain manipulation using supported case observations; do not invent a universal timing cutoff.

answerChoices.rationale: An initial reoperation is more invasive than correcting accessible drainage in this stable patient without generalized contamination.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After food-linked pancrelipase, stools improve and weight stabilizes. Disabling epigastric pain persists. Prior stone extraction and repeated pancreatic-duct stent exchanges gave only brief relief. Current MRI shows a 9-mm main duct with a recurrent dominant stricture and intraductal stones extending through the body. The head is not enlarged, and no focal mass is seen. He remains fit for pancreatic surgery.
decisionNodes.stem: Which intervention should be discussed for {patientName}'s persistent pancreatic pain now?

answerChoices.rationale: Repeated endoscopic attempts have not achieved durable relief; another identical cycle is less appropriate than surgery in this candidate.

answerChoices.rationale: A block may palliate selected patients but does not address the demonstrated obstructed duct after failed decompression.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The returned pancreatic MRI describes side-branch cysts communicating with the main duct, a main duct measuring 11 mm and a 7-mm enhancing mural nodule in the head lesion. Staging shows no distant lesion. {patientName} walks independently and her cardiopulmonary assessment supports major surgery.
decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s pancreatic cyst findings now?

answerChoices.label: Continue MRI-based cyst surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Routine surveillance is insufficient for the combined high-risk findings in a surgical candidate.

answerChoices.label: Arrange EUS-guided cyst-fluid sampling
answerChoices.rationale: Sampling can help unresolved risk classification, but the MRI already supplies two independently high-risk findings. Negative fluid would not erase them.

answerChoices.label: Refer for oncologic pancreatic-head resection
answerChoices.rationale: A fit patient with this duct and enhancing-nodule pattern needs multidisciplinary planning for pancreatic resection.

decisionNodes.explanation: Duct communication suggests an IPMN pathway. The duct and enhancing nodule meet high-risk criteria, so surgical evaluation is indicated in this fit patient. These findings do not prove invasive cancer, and the final resection extent belongs to the pancreatic multidisciplinary team.

cases.presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old woman, attends clinic to review outside records after her first pancreatitis admission. The chart labels a body-tail cyst present two years before the attack as A and a new lesser-sac collection as B.

approvedInstantiationProfiles.presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old woman, attends clinic to review outside records after her first pancreatitis admission. The chart labels a body-tail cyst present two years before the attack as A and a new lesser-sac collection as B.

sourceLabels: ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Pancreatic Cysts
Pancreatic cystic lesions: SIRM-AISP position paper

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Subsequent MRI and EUS show A as a 4.6-cm septated body-tail cyst without duct communication. It indents the stomach; endoscopy shows intact mucosa over the indentation. Meal-related fullness continues after B has resolved. Fluid CEA is markedly elevated; cytology contains scant mucinous epithelium without identified high-grade atypia. She has no major operative comorbidity.
decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s lesion A after this assessment?

answerChoices.label: Continue MRI surveillance of lesion A
answerChoices.rationale: Scant cytology without high-grade atypia cannot establish low whole-lesion risk. The large lesion and persistent compressive symptoms favor surgical evaluation.

answerChoices.label: Refer A for distal pancreatic resection
answerChoices.rationale: The morphology supports presumed MCN, and size plus persistent gastric compression support resection consideration in a fit patient without requiring proof of cancer.

answerChoices.label: Repeat EUS sampling of lesion A
answerChoices.rationale: Another sample may add information but a negative result would not remove the current size and symptom indications for surgical evaluation. Demonstrating invasive cancer is not a prerequisite for referral.

decisionNodes.explanation: The combined location, lack of duct communication and mucinous fluid assessment favor presumed MCN rather than establish its histology. A's size and persistent gastric compression support resection evaluation. CEA does not diagnose invasive cancer, and scant bland cells do not establish safety. Repeat sampling need not delay referral when the decision already rests on size and symptoms.
sourceLabels: ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Pancreatic Cysts
Pancreatic cystic lesions: SIRM-AISP position paper

cases.presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old man, attends clinic to review outside surveillance records for a nonfunctioning pancreatic-body neuroendocrine tumor initially measuring 8 mm.

approvedInstantiationProfiles.presentation: {patientName}, a 72-year-old man, attends clinic to review outside surveillance records for a nonfunctioning pancreatic-body neuroendocrine tumor initially measuring 8 mm.

sourceLabels: NANETS surgical management of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
NCI PDQ pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors treatment

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A later surveillance record shows the body lesion has grown to 2.8 cm. EUS places its deep margin 1 mm from the main duct, with new upstream dilation. Repeat staging shows no distant disease. The original small biopsy had a low proliferation index. Updated cardiopulmonary assessment supports pancreatic resection.
decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s pancreatic tumor now?

answerChoices.label: Continue pancreatic imaging surveillance
answerChoices.rationale: Actual growth and new ductal effect override the previous low-risk surveillance premise.

answerChoices.label: Enucleation of the pancreatic body lesion
answerChoices.rationale: This larger deep lesion lies close to the main duct; enucleation risks duct injury and does not provide the same regional assessment.

answerChoices.label: Distal pancreatectomy with regional node assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Growth, larger size and duct proximity favor formal resection rather than continued observation or enucleation.

decisionNodes.explanation: The later tumor is no longer the lesion for which surveillance was selected. Growth and an upstream duct effect create a new management problem. Its deep margin is too close to the main duct for the favorable enucleation criteria; formal resection with regional assessment is the appropriate offered operation. A limited old sample cannot freeze future risk assessment.
sourceLabels: NANETS surgical management of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
NCI PDQ pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors treatment

cases.presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old man, attends clinic after pancreatic-neck lesion enucleation. The founder reviews an outside hospital readmission record documenting a postoperative collection and an operative drain.

sourceLabels: Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for chronic pancreatitis 2021
Management of complications occurring after pancreatic surgery

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Later in the same admission, fresh blood briefly appears in the drain and then stops. Hemoglobin falls. The collection had contained enzyme-rich fluid. There is no hematemesis or melena, and circulation is currently maintained.
decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should be obtained urgently in {patientName}'s hospital record after this bleeding episode?

answerChoices.label: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: The observed extraluminal drain bleeding favors evaluation of a postoperative vascular source rather than an initial mucosal examination.

answerChoices.label: MRI with MRCP of the pancreatic duct
answerChoices.rationale: Duct mapping does not identify and control an urgent arterial bleeding risk.

answerChoices.label: CT angiography of the abdomen
answerChoices.rationale: A transient drain bleed after pancreatic surgery can be a sentinel event; urgent vascular imaging can direct endovascular treatment in a stable patient.

decisionNodes.explanation: Cessation does not make this episode reassuring. Postoperative pancreatic leakage can be associated with vascular erosion and later major hemorrhage. In the currently stable record, urgent CT angiography can identify a source for endovascular treatment. This is a review of hospital-level care; the clinic does not execute it.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At readmission, vomiting and abdominal fullness recur after initial oral intake. Temperature and white-cell count rise. Previously enzyme-rich drain output abruptly decreases. Blood pressure is maintained and there is no generalized guarding.
decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should have been obtained next in {patientName}'s outside-hospital record?

answerChoices.label: Radionuclide gastric-emptying study
answerChoices.rationale: A functional emptying test does not first address systemic inflammation and possible inadequately drained postoperative fluid.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis
answerChoices.rationale: Cross-sectional evaluation is needed to investigate a postoperative collection or other secondary complication.

answerChoices.label: Pancreatic MRI with MRCP
answerChoices.rationale: Duct mapping may later inform persistent leakage, but the immediate unresolved issue is a new inflammatory abdominal complication.

decisionNodes.explanation: Vomiting after pancreatic surgery should not be assigned to isolated delayed emptying while systemic inflammation and changing drain behavior suggest a secondary complication. CT is the appropriate offered initial assessment of the current abdomen. Duct mapping or functional testing addresses different remaining questions.
